title: Wireless Collaborative Inference Acceleration Based on Distillation for Weed Detection and Instance Segmentation
evidence_summary: The paper proposes a wireless collaborative inference framework (improved Mask R-CNN with backbone feature fusion, Soft-NMS, refined mask branch, knowledge distillation, and two-stage model partition) for weed detection and instance segmentation on resource-limited weeding robots. In Section IV-A (Dataset, p. 5), the authors take the existing CWD30 crop-weed dataset [22], filter for high-quality images, split 6:2:2, apply augmentations, and add 1,120 self-collected samples, yielding 9,520 images across 34 crop/weed classes with instance masks annotated in LabelMe and formatted in COCO. This extended dataset is used for training, validation, and testing: the improved Mask R-CNN is compared against Mask R-CNN, DeepMask, and MNC on the full test set (Table I, p. 6; F1 0.918, AP50 0.730), and knowledge-distillation results appear in Table II (p. 6; mAP 0.617). A drone-server field test in a real farmland environment (Section IV-D, Figs. 15-16) validates the framework; the paper does not state release of the derived dataset.

evidence_summary: This IROS 2025 paper (University of Bonn) proposes WaW ('Weeds are Weird'), a zero-shot, label-free crop-weed semantic segmentation method that frames weeds as anomalies: it curates a bag-of-features of crop plants using foundation models SAM and BioCLIP and classifies vegetation segments outside the crop-feature manifold as weeds (Fig. 1, p. 1; Sec. title: A 3D Surface Reconstruction Pipeline for Plant Phenotyping

evidence_summary: The paper presents CropMesh, an automated open-source pipeline (github.com/Engineering-Geodesy-Bonn/CropMesh, implemented in Open3D) that converts high-resolution 3D point clouds into triangular-mesh surface models for plant phenotyping via statistical outlier removal, voxel sub-sampling, ball-pivoting reconstruction, Taubin smoothing, and hole filling (Section 2, p. 4). The authors collect three new datasets: (1) laboratory point clouds of four plants (banana, bow hemp, money tree, philodendron) scanned with a handheld arm scanner at 12 µm minimum resolution plus flatbed-scanner leaf-area references (Section 3.1, pp. 8-9, Figures 4-5); (2) a single field soybean plant scanned on seven dates in 2021 with a mobile mapping robot (Section 3.2, pp. 9-10, Figures 6, 10); and (3) soybean plots of two varieties (Eiko, Minngold) at two densities scanned with a Leica ScanStation P50 TLS on 12 July and 10 August 2022 (Section 3.2, pp. 10-11, Figures 7-8). The pipeline is evaluated on all three datasets (Section 4, pp. 12-15): reconstructed-mesh leaf areas agree with flatbed references within 6.42% (Table 1, p. 13), seasonal plant growth is tracked (Figure 10, p. 14), and leaf angle distributions differ by variety and measurement time (Figure 12, p. 15). The datasets are unnamed and available only on request (Data Availability Statement, p. 17).

evidence_summary: The paper introduces a self-collected dataset of 1000 maize seedling images (three-to-five-leaf stage) captured with an iPhone XS (1920x1080) at 60 cm height in a Zibo, Shandong test field at three day periods, resized to 512x512, maize seedlings polygon-labeled with labelme v5.2.1 in PASCAL VOC 2007 format, split 7:2:1 into train/test/val (Sec. 2.1, pp. 2-3; Figure 1, p.3), with the training set augmented 5x (Sec. 2.2, p.3). The dataset is not publicly released; the Data Availability Statement (p.14) offers data on reasonable request from the corresponding author.

evidence_summary: The paper introduces WeedGraphNet, a knowledge-guided refinement framework for late-season rice-weed segmentation from UAV RGB orthomosaics: a compact U-Net generates an initial map that is refined with vegetation gating (dark-pixel safeguard), soft chromatic priors, and crop-row geometric constraints (Sections 3.2-3.3). It releases a self-collected dataset of 420 tiles (400 training / 20 validation, 512x512 px, classes rice/weed/others, 1,384,278 labeled pixels) from a single 25 July 2025 DJI Mavic 3 Multispectral RGB campaign at Jiu Farm, Anqing, China, split with a leakage-safe blocked spatial protocol (Sections 2.4-2.6; Table 2, pp. 4-5). The framework is trained and evaluated on these held-out tiles, reaching OA = 0.9742, Macro-F1 = 0.9368, and mIoU = 0.8833, with ablation (A0-A4) and morphological-baseline comparisons (Section 4.1; Tables 3-6; Fig. 5, pp. 7-8). The field datasets are unnamed and the paper provides no data-availability statement or release mechanism, so the contribution is the method rather than a reusable dataset.

title: Rapid, high-resolution measurement of leaf area and leaf orientation using terrestrial LiDAR scanning data
evidence_summary: This paper develops a new method to simultaneously measure leaf area density (LAD) and the leaf orientation p.d.f. from terrestrial LiDAR scans, computing the G-function (fraction of projected leaf area) directly from triangulated scan data and inverting the Beer-Lambert law with radiation transfer theory rather than the point-quadrat analogy (Abstract; Secs. 2.2-2.5, pp. 5-9). Validation used (1) synthetic computer-generated LiDAR data with circular disks of known geometry (4 disk densities x 20 realizations; Sec. 3.1, pp. 10-13; Figs. 4-6) and (2) field scans of a single black cottonwood tree (Populus balsamifera) in Oregon with destructive leaf-area reference measurements in 6 of 12 voxels (Sec. 3.2, pp. 13-18; Figs. 7-9). Agreement was good: nRMSE ~15% for the synthetic tests and ~13% in the field, with the Eq. 10 radiation-transfer inversion giving index of agreement d=0.98 and +0.30 m2 bias (Table 3, p. 18; parameter values in Table 2, p. 17). No dataset is introduced or released (no data-availability statement) and no existing agricultural CV dataset is used; all data are experiment-specific synthetic and single-tree field scans.

title: RPD: Learning Efficient Crops and Weeds for Field Semantic Segmentation in Drone Images
evidence_summary: RPD-Net, a lightweight reparameterized pixel-difference network for crop/weed semantic segmentation in drone imagery, is trained from scratch and evaluated on two public drone-acquired datasets: PhenoBench [3] (sugarbeet, ~21 m flight height, 1 mm/px GSD, classes crops/weeds/soil) and CoFly-WeedDB [21] (cotton, ~5 m flight height, 1.4-1.6 mm/px GSD, classes Johnson grass/purslane/field bindweed + background) (Section IV-A, p.5, Table I). Models are trained from scratch on the official PhenoBench training split and evaluated on its validation split as the primary benchmark, with ablations and SOTA comparisons reported there (Section IV-A/B/C, pp.5-10, Tables II-VII, Figs. 4-6). For CoFly, the 201 images are split 8:2 (161 train/40 val), cropped into 256x256 patches, and augmented to 1,878 training samples for binary and multiclass weed segmentation (Section IV-D, p.10, Table VIII; results Tables IX-X, Fig. 7, pp.11-12). No new dataset is introduced; code is released at github.com/chenfh21/RPD-Net (Abstract, p.1).

title: AgriSeg: A Comprehensive Study on Semantic Segmentation for Leaf Disease, Fruit, and Crop-Weed Detection
evidence_summary: AgriSeg is a benchmarking study (not a new dataset) that trains and evaluates five semantic segmentation models (DeepLabv3+, SegNeXt, PD-SegNet, InternImage, meta-prompts) on five existing public agricultural CV datasets - NLB, LDSD, MinneApple, WGISD, and CWFID - covering leaf disease, fruit, and crop-weed tasks (Abstract, p. 1; Section III-A, p. 3). Per-dataset train/test splits are specified (e.g., NLB 845 train/100 test, MinneApple 670/371, WGISD 110/27, CWFID 40 train/20 test; Section III-A, p. 3), and all models are trained at 512x512 on the MMSegmentation codebase with stated hyper-parameters (Section III-C, p. 4). Quantitative results (mIoU, Acc, per-class IoU) for each dataset are reported in Tables I-III (p. 4), with qualitative comparisons in Figs. 3-4 (p. 5); the study sets SOTA benchmarks and documents ground-truth annotation errors in existing datasets (Section IV-B, p. 5).

title: An Efficient Weed Detection Model using RCNN and YOLO Algorithms
named_datasets: Crop and Weed Detection Data with Bounding Boxes (Kaggle)
evidence_summary: The paper trains weed-vs-crop classification (pre-trained ResNet50 via transfer learning) and weed detection (YOLOv5 and RCNN) models for sesame fields using an existing public Kaggle dataset of crop/weed images with bounding boxes (ref [11]; Section III, p.2; Section IV.A, p.3). The authors report curating the data from 589 recorded images to 546 after cleaning, then augmenting to 1,300 YOLO-format images resized to 512x512 (Section IV.A, p.3); bounding-box crops were used to train the ResNet50 classifier with 70/20/10 train/validation/test splits (Section IV.C, p.3-4). YOLOv5 and RCNN were trained for 100 epochs on the annotated images and compared in Section IV.D; Table 1 (p.5) and Figures 3-6 (p.4-5) report YOLOv5 at mAP@0.5 0.987 with 0.02 s/image inference vs RCNN 0.981 at 0.5 s/image. No new dataset is released; the study applies standard models to a well-known existing dataset.

title: Weed and Crop Detection Using YOLOv7: A Step Toward Smarter Precision Agriculture
evidence_summary: This single-author conference paper trains and evaluates YOLOv7 (a custom unofficial implementation, later YOLOv7-tiny) for binary crop/weed detection on the CropAndWeed dataset of the Austrian Institute of Technology (Section I, p. 1: approx. 8,000 images at 1920x1088 px, over 111,000 annotated instances from 929 field sessions, approx. 12 GB, with bounding-box/segmentation/stem-coordinate annotations). It trains on the CropAndWeed2 subset (all crop species collapsed to one superclass, all weeds to another), preprocesses/augments (329 negative samples, approx. 4%; Pascal-VOC to YOLO tensor conversion; resize to 640 or 1280 px), and splits 75:15:15 train/val/test (Section III, p. 3). Evaluation reports test loss 1.22 and mAP 0.48 at IoU 0.7, with final precision of 70-85% mostly for crops (Section IV, p. 4; Fig. 2; Fig. 4; Fig. 5). No dataset is introduced; CropAndWeed is used as an existing public dataset.
source_section: Section I (dataset description); Section III (CropAndWeed2 training); Section IV (results)
